meta.title: Elements of Banking
meta.description: Access Bank Entry Level Training Program: banking business, functions, products, financial structure, and regulation, updated for the CBN's 2024 recapitalization requirements.

modules.title: Income Sources and Financial Structure of Banks

questionBank.q: Under Nigeria's banking regulatory framework, what makes an institution accurately describable as a "Bank"?
opts: It has been designated a Domestically Systemically Important Bank by the regulator.
It has been licensed to carry out the business of banking.
It has satisfied the Central Bank of Nigeria's minimum paid-up capital requirement.
It operates under the Central Bank of Nigeria's Non-Interest Financial Institutions framework.
questionBank.exp: A bank is, by definition, an institution licensed to carry out the business of banking — the license itself is the defining criterion, not any single attribute a bank happens to also have. Meeting the minimum capital requirement (option C) is one precondition for obtaining that license, but capital alone doesn't confer bank status without the license being granted. D-SIB designation and the Non-Interest Financial Institutions framework are both real regulatory categories, but they classify a subset of already-licensed banks rather than defining what a bank is in the first place.

questionBank.q: Which of the following activities is included within the Central Bank of Nigeria's definition of banking business?
opts: Underwriting insurance policies for individual policyholders
Advising clients on corporate and investment matters
Adjusting losses following an insured event
Reinsuring risks for primary insurance companies
questionBank.exp: The CBN's definition of banking business explicitly includes consultancy and advisory services relating to corporate and investment matters. Insurance underwriting, loss adjusting, and re-insurance are all real financial-sector services, but banks are specifically barred from providing insurance underwriting, loss adjusting, or re-insurance services — the opposite of being part of banking business.

questionBank.q: A customer notices her bank pays 4% interest on her savings account but charges 18% on personal loans. Which principle explains why the bank sets these two rates at different levels?
opts: The bank profits from fees and commissions charged on e-channel transactions.
The bank profits from the spread between deposit and loan interest rates.
The bank profits from dividends and capital gains earned on treasury bill investments.
The bank profits from income generated through foreign exchange trading.
questionBank.exp: Banks accept deposits and make loans, deriving profit from the spread between the interest rate paid to depositors and the interest rate charged to borrowers — this is the core mechanism behind the rate gap the customer observed. E-channel fees, investment income, and FX trading income are all real but separate income sources that don't explain this particular rate differential.

questionBank.q: What is the relationship between the degree of trust the banking system elicits and the system's overall stability?
opts: Trust and stability move independently of one another within the banking system.
A higher degree of trust produces greater stability and a healthier banking system.
Excessive public trust weakens banking stability by encouraging reckless lending.
Trust primarily affects a bank's profitability rather than its overall stability.
questionBank.exp: The stated principle is that the higher the degree of trust the banking system can elicit, the greater its stability and the healthier it is — trust and stability move together, not independently, and trust is framed as foundational to stability rather than to profitability alone.

questionBank.q: A goldsmith authorizes payment of a stated sum to whoever presents a signed note from one of his depositors. Which modern banking instrument did this practice most directly evolve into?
opts: The certificate of deposit
The cheque
The letter of credit
The bankers' acceptance
questionBank.exp: This practice — a goldsmith paying the bearer of a depositor's authorizing note — is described as the direct forerunner of the modern cheque. Certificates of deposit, letters of credit, and bankers' acceptances are all genuine banking instruments discussed elsewhere, but none trace their origin to this specific bearer-payment practice.

questionBank.q: Goldsmiths began issuing more receipts than the gold actually held in their vaults, using the surplus receipts to extend loans at interest. What banking function did this practice originate?
opts: The foreign exchange market
Money creation
Deposit insurance
The cash reserve requirement
questionBank.exp: Issuing receipts beyond the gold actually held, then lending out the surplus, is described as the origin of money creation as an integral part of banking. The foreign exchange market, deposit insurance, and the cash reserve requirement are all real banking concepts covered elsewhere, but none originate from this specific goldsmith practice.

questionBank.q: A goldsmith's outstanding receipts eventually exceed the gold physically held in his vault. What does this imply about the receipts still in circulation?
opts: Each receipt's value is adjusted daily to reflect the market price of gold.
Some of the receipts in circulation are not backed by physical gold.
Depositors are repaid strictly according to the order in which their gold was deposited.
The excess receipts are formally registered by the goldsmith as a separate currency.
questionBank.exp: If total receipts outstanding exceed the gold in the vault, simple arithmetic means some receipts cannot be matched to actual gold — this is the fictitious, unbacked paper described as the start of money creation. Daily revaluation, strict repayment ordering, and formal separate-currency registration are all specific claims the material never supports.

questionBank.q: A newly licensed deposit-taking institution wants to strengthen the public trust that underpins banking stability during its first year of operation. Based on the relationship between trust and stability, which practice would most directly serve that goal?
opts: Prioritizing rapid growth of its loan portfolio to maximize interest income.
Maintaining sufficient liquidity to reliably meet depositors' withdrawal demands.
Expanding its branch network as quickly as possible to increase visibility.
Offering the highest deposit interest rates available in the market.
questionBank.exp: Trust in banking rests on depositors' confidence that they can get their money back when they want it — reliably meeting withdrawal demand is what directly sustains that confidence. Aggressive loan growth, branch expansion, and rate competition are all plausible growth strategies, but none directly address the trust-stability link described above; aggressive loan growth in particular can work against it by straining the institution's ability to meet withdrawals.

questionBank.q: Under the CBN's New Banking Model, how are Commercial Banks, Specialised Banks, and Merchant Banks related to one another?
opts: Merchant Banks are a subcategory nested within Specialised Banks.
They are three separate categories that sit directly beneath the CBN's New Banking Model.
Commercial Banks are licensed only as a subset of Merchant Banks.
Non-Interest Financial Institutions sit directly beneath the New Banking Model, alongside Commercial Banks.
questionBank.exp: The CBN's New Banking Model splits directly into three parallel categories: Commercial Banks, Specialised Banks, and Merchant Banks. Non-Interest Financial Institutions sit two levels down, nested inside Specialised Banks — not directly beneath the New Banking Model — and neither Merchant nor Commercial Banks is a subset of the other.

questionBank.q: A promoter is setting up a new deposit-taking bank in Nigeria that will also operate branches in three other West African countries. What minimum paid-up capital must this bank hold to be licensed as a Commercial Bank?
opts: N50 billion
N500 billion
N200 billion
N20 billion
questionBank.exp: Under the CBN's 2024 recapitalization requirements, Commercial Banks operating internationally must hold a minimum paid-up capital of N500 billion — higher than the N200 billion required of a national Commercial Bank or the N50 billion required of a regional one. N20 billion is the minimum capital for a National Non-Interest Bank, a different licence category entirely.

questionBank.q: Which institution type sits under Non-Interest Financial Institutions within the Specialised Banks branch of the CBN's New Banking Model?
opts: The Development Banks category
The Islamic Financial Institutions category
The Merchant Banks category
The Commercial Banks category
questionBank.exp: Islamic Financial Institutions sit within the Non-Interest Financial Institutions branch of Specialised Banks. Development Banks sit in the separate Microfinance/Development/Primary Mortgage Institutions branch of Specialised Banks, while Merchant Banks and Commercial Banks are entirely separate top-level categories, not nested under Specialised Banks at all.

questionBank.q: Which statement best distinguishes a Community Bank from a Microfinance Bank, based on their respective roles?
opts: A Microfinance Bank serves a defined neighbourhood, while a Community Bank serves the broader mass retail market.
A Community Bank serves a defined neighbourhood, while a Microfinance Bank serves the broader mass retail market.
A Community Bank underwrites long-term international finance, while a Microfinance Bank focuses on wholesale banking.
A Community Bank underwrites equity and debt issues, while a Microfinance Bank cannot accept deposits withdrawable by cheque.
questionBank.exp: Community Banks collect deposits from and lend to members of a defined neighbourhood or cell, while Microfinance Banks are geared towards intermediation for the lower end of the retail (mass) market — a broader population than a single neighbourhood. The first distractor simply reverses these two roles; the other two borrow facts that actually describe Merchant Banks, not either institution named here.

questionBank.q: One financial institution's core service is underwriting, acting as intermediary between securities issuers and the investing public, and facilitating mergers. A separate institution's core mandate is funding new and upcoming businesses as part of regional economic development projects. Which classification correctly labels the first institution?
opts: A Development Bank
An Investment Bank
A Merchant Bank
A Central Bank
questionBank.exp: Underwriting, acting as intermediary between securities issuers and investors, and facilitating mergers are the defining services of an Investment Bank. The description of funding new businesses for regional economic development instead matches a Development Bank — picking it here would mean swapping the two institutions' descriptions. Merchant Banks and Central Banks are real categories but neither matches the services described for the first institution.

questionBank.q: A customer walks into a Merchant Bank and asks to open a current account from which she can withdraw funds by writing cheques for everyday expenses. Based on the regulatory distinction between Merchant Banks and Commercial Banks, how should the bank respond?
opts: Accept the request, since Merchant Banks specialize in retail current accounts.
Decline the request, since Merchant Banks cannot accept deposits withdrawable by cheque.
Accept the request, but only once she deposits a minimum of ₦100 million.
Accept the request, since Commercial Banks and Merchant Banks share identical deposit rules.
questionBank.exp: Merchant Banks cannot accept deposits withdrawable by cheque, so the request must be declined regardless of deposit size — the ₦100 million figure is a real Merchant Bank requirement, but it applies to minimum deposits generally, not to unlocking cheque-withdrawable accounts, which Merchant Banks are barred from offering outright. Retail current accounts and cheque withdrawal are Commercial Bank features, and the two bank types' deposit rules are explicitly different, not identical.

questionBank.q: A company wants a single bank to both grant it a working-capital credit facility and underwrite its planned bond issuance on the capital market. Based on the regulatory distinction between Merchant Banks and Commercial Banks, what does this requirement imply?
opts: A Commercial Bank alone can meet both needs, since it may grant loans and also underwrites securities.
A Merchant Bank alone can meet both needs, since it may grant corporate credit facilities and also underwrite securities.
No bank can meet both needs, since both Merchant and Commercial Banks are barred from underwriting securities.
Either bank type can meet both needs, since underwriting and lending rules apply equally to Merchant and Commercial Banks.
questionBank.exp: Merchant Banks may grant credit facilities and are also permitted to underwrite equity and debt issues, so a single Merchant Bank can meet both needs. Commercial Banks can grant loans but are explicitly barred from underwriting issues, so they cannot meet the second need; the claim that both banks are barred from underwriting, or that the rules apply equally to both, misstates the actual asymmetry between the two categories.

questionBank.q: A client needs a bank that can both provide treasury management services and deal directly in foreign exchange, and is deciding between a Merchant Bank and a Commercial Bank. Which consideration should most directly settle the client's choice?
opts: Only a Commercial Bank can offer treasury management, so it is the only qualifying option.
Neither service distinguishes them, since both bank types offer treasury management and foreign exchange services.
Only a Merchant Bank can deal directly in foreign exchange, so it is the only qualifying option.
Neither bank type offers foreign exchange services, so the client must look outside the banking sector.
questionBank.exp: Treasury management and foreign exchange dealing are both listed among the services Merchant Banks and Commercial Banks share, so neither criterion actually narrows the choice between them — the client needs a different, distinguishing consideration (such as whether they also need cheque-withdrawable deposits or capital-market underwriting) to decide. Assuming either service is exclusive to one bank type would be a factual error the similarities list directly contradicts.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the bulk source of commercial bank funds?
opts: Borrowings
Deposits
Equity capital
Spontaneous finance
questionBank.exp: The bulk of commercial bank funds comes from deposits — demand, savings, and time deposits together. Borrowings, equity capital, and spontaneous finance are all real non-deposit sources of funds, but each supplies only a minor portion of total funds compared with deposits.

questionBank.q: Which deposit type is described as forming the basis for credit and debit card usage and electronic funds transfers?
opts: Savings deposits
Demand deposits
Non-negotiable CDs
Negotiable CDs
questionBank.exp: Demand deposits — current or checking accounts — are described as forming the basis for using credit and debit cards and electronic transfers, in addition to being a safe, widely accepted means of payment. Savings deposits and certificates of deposit serve different purposes and aren't linked to card-based or electronic payment infrastructure in the material.

questionBank.q: Which statement accurately describes savings deposits, as distinct from demand and time deposits?
opts: They are generally traded in the money market and bear a negotiable interest rate.
They are generally small, earn low interest, and can be withdrawn with no notice.
They form the basis for credit and debit card usage and electronic transfers.
They are usually small, consumer-type accounts that cannot be traded before maturity.
questionBank.exp: Savings deposits are generally small amounts that bear a relatively low interest rate and may be withdrawn by the depositor with no notice. Trading in the money market describes negotiable CDs, card/electronic-transfer usage describes demand deposits, and being untradeable before maturity describes non-negotiable CDs — all real facts, but each misattributed to savings deposits here.

questionBank.q: A bank issues two certificates of deposit of the same value: one is a small, consumer-type instrument, and the other can be actively traded by other parties before it matures. What distinguishes the second certificate from the first?
opts: The second is a demand deposit, which permits withdrawal by cheque, unlike the first, a time deposit.
The second is a negotiable CD, which may be traded in the money market, unlike the first, a non-negotiable CD.
The second earns no interest as a non-earning cash reserve, unlike the first, which is interest-bearing.
The second is a savings deposit withdrawable without notice, unlike the first, which is a fixed time deposit.
questionBank.exp: Time deposits split into non-negotiable CDs, which are small consumer-type accounts, and negotiable CDs, which may be traded in the money market before maturity — exactly the two instruments described. The other options each reassign the scenario to a different, unrelated deposit or asset category the material does not support here.

questionBank.q: A bank issues corporate bonds to raise additional funding as competition for customer deposits intensifies. Which non-deposit source of funds does this represent?
opts: Spontaneous finance
Borrowings
Equity capital
Demand deposits
questionBank.exp: Bonds and debentures are cited as examples of borrowings — a non-deposit funding source banks increasingly rely on as deposit competition rises. Spontaneous finance arises from day-to-day current liabilities rather than deliberate issuance, equity capital comes from shareholders, and demand deposits are a deposit source, not a non-deposit one.

questionBank.q: A bank channels funds directly to a deficit-sector customer through a term loan. What type of obligation does this create for the bank?
opts: A secondary obligation, as with underwriting
A primary obligation
A secondary obligation, as with a guarantee
A contingent obligation recorded off the bank's balance sheet
questionBank.exp: Direct lending creates a primary obligation for the bank, since it channels funds straight to the borrower. Underwriting and guarantees are both classified as secondary obligations instead, and off-balance-sheet contingent obligations describe instruments like letters of credit and performance bonds, not a direct term loan.

questionBank.q: A bank is comparing the risk and return profile of its direct lending, underwriting, and guarantee activities. Direct lending carries the highest risk among the three. What best explains its correspondingly higher return?
opts: It earns brokerage fees exclusively, unlike underwriting and guarantee, which earn interest spread.
It earns an interest spread plus high credit-related fees, exceeding underwriting's brokerage fees and guarantee's fees-only return.
It earns a flat fee only, with no interest spread, unlike underwriting and guarantee.
It earns interest spread only, identical to underwriting's return, with guarantee earning nothing.
questionBank.exp: Direct lending's return combines an interest spread with high credit-related fees, which is a richer return than underwriting's interest spread plus brokerage fees, or guarantee's fees-only return. Underwriting also earns an interest spread, so treating direct lending as the only method earning one is the specific error in the last two distractors.

questionBank.q: A corporate client is issuing commercial paper to the investing public and wants its bank to evaluate, approve, and stand behind the risk of default on the issue — without the bank disbursing loan funds directly to the client up front. Which of the bank's three credit-granting methods best fits this requirement?
opts: Direct Lending
Underwriting
Guarantee
A performance bond arrangement
questionBank.exp: Underwriting is defined as a bank evaluating, approving, and undertaking the risk of loss or default, fully or in part, on a customer's issue — exactly what this commercial-paper scenario describes, and commercial paper is itself the given example of an underwritten instrument. Direct lending would mean disbursing funds up front, which the scenario rules out; a guarantee backs a third-party lender rather than standing behind the client's own securities issue; and a performance bond is a specific example of a guarantee, not underwriting.

questionBank.q: Under the qualified-borrower framework, which three factors combine to indicate a borrower's willingness to repay?
opts: Capital, Competence, and Cash Flow
Character, Collateral, and Connection
Character, Competence, and Conditions External
Collateral, Cash Flow, and Conditions External
questionBank.exp: Willingness is assessed through Character, Collateral, and Connection. Capital, Competence, and Cash Flow instead sit under Ability, and Conditions External is its own separate category — mixing factors across these three groups produces each of the wrong options.

questionBank.q: Under the qualified-borrower framework, which three factors combine to indicate a borrower's ability to repay?
opts: Character, Collateral, and Connection
Capital, Competence, and Cash Flow
Conditions External alone
Character, Cash Flow, and Conditions External
questionBank.exp: Ability is assessed through Capital/Equity contributions, Competence, and Cash Flow. Character, Collateral, and Connection instead sit under Willingness, and Conditions External is a distinct single-factor category on its own, not a stand-in for the three Ability factors.

questionBank.q: A loan officer notes that a borrower has strong personal integrity and reliable connections in the business community, but is unsure whether the borrower's cash flow can service the facility. Which two elements of the qualified-borrower framework does this observation span?
opts: Willingness and Conditions External
Willingness and Ability
Ability and Conditions External
Conditions External on its own
questionBank.exp: Personal integrity and business connections are Character and Connection, both Willingness factors, while cash flow sufficiency sits under Ability — so the observation spans Willingness and Ability. Pairing either category with Conditions External, or citing Conditions External alone, misassigns the specific factors actually named in the scenario.

questionBank.q: Approximately what proportion of a bank's total asset base do loans and advances typically form?
opts: About 45%
About 50%
About 65%
About 30%
questionBank.exp: Loans and advances form about 50% of a bank's asset base. 65% is instead the figure for direct revenue once credit-related fees are included, 45% is the Cash Reserve Ratio for Commercial Banks, and 30% is the minimum liquidity ratio — all real figures from elsewhere in the material, but none describing asset-base composition.

questionBank.q: A bank's management is deciding where to focus growth efforts to boost operating revenue most significantly. Based on banks' typical income contributors, which activity should be prioritized?
opts: Growing custodial services revenue, since safekeeping fees form the largest share of operating revenue.
Growing the loan and advances portfolio, since loans typically provide the largest share of a bank's operating revenue.
Growing foreign exchange trading income, since FX transactions form the largest share of operating revenue.
Growing rental income from bank-owned property, since rental income forms the largest share of operating revenue.
questionBank.exp: Loans — including money market advances — provide the largest portion of a traditional bank's operating revenue, typically above 50% of direct revenue. Custodial fees, FX income, and rental income are all real income sources described elsewhere, but none is identified as the largest contributor.

questionBank.q: A bank experiences a wave of non-performing credits across its loan portfolio. Given that loans are often described as a bank's "survival skill," what does this situation most directly threaten?
opts: The bank's foreign exchange income only, since survival skill relates specifically to currency trading.
The bank's continued survival, since non-performing credits are described as the fastest way to "kill" a bank.
The bank's custodial services fees only, since survival skill relates specifically to safekeeping.
Nothing directly, since survival skill refers only to a bank's ability to open new branches.
questionBank.exp: It is stated plainly that the fastest way to "kill" a bank is through non-performing credits, since each loan teaches a bank either how to extend a facility or how not to — making loan quality central to survival itself, not to any single income line like FX trading, custodial fees, or branch expansion.

questionBank.q: Which set correctly lists the three bases on which bank customers can be categorized?
opts: Corporate strategy, net cash flow generation, and minimum paid-up capital
Corporate strategy, net cash flow generation, and volume of business activities
Net cash flow generation, volume of business activities, and licensing category
Corporate strategy, volume of business activities, and capital adequacy ratio
questionBank.exp: Customers are categorized by corporate strategy (Corporate/Commercial/Consumer), by net cash flow generation (Borrowing/Deposit customers), and by volume of business activities (Wholesale/Retail). Minimum paid-up capital, licensing category, and capital adequacy ratio are all real regulatory concepts from elsewhere, but none is used as a customer-segmentation basis.

questionBank.q: A company reports an annual gross turnover of N6 billion and approaches Access Bank for financing. Which of the bank's four customer segments should handle this relationship?
opts: Corporates
Commercial
Business Banking
Personal Banking
questionBank.exp: Access Bank's Commercial segment covers institutions and corporates with annual gross turnover between N1 billion and N10 billion, which N6 billion falls within. Corporates requires a minimum turnover of N10 billion, so N6 billion falls short of that threshold; Business Banking caps out at N1 billion, well below this company's turnover; and Personal Banking serves individuals, not companies.

questionBank.q: Zenith Trust Bank receives a fresh deposit of N200,000 from a customer. If the bank sets aside a 10% Cash Reserve Ratio and a 15% liquidity reserve against the deposit, how much of the N200,000 is available to the bank as cash after both reserves are set aside?
questionBank.exp: CRR = 10% x N200,000 = N20,000; liquidity reserve = 15% x N200,000 = N30,000; cash = N200,000 − N20,000 − N30,000 = N150,000 (75% of the deposit) — mirroring the worked illustration above, where a N100,000 deposit splits into N10,000 CRR, N15,000 liquidity reserve, and N75,000 cash. N180,000 and N170,000 each deduct only one reserve instead of both, and N100,000 mistakenly deducts the combined 25% reserve twice.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an example of Direct Lending, one of the three ways banks grant credit?
opts: Commercial paper
Import Finance Facility
Banker's acceptance
Advance payment guarantee
questionBank.exp: Import Finance Facility is listed as an example of Direct Lending, alongside overdrafts, term loans, and trade finance. Commercial paper and banker's acceptances are Underwriting examples instead, and an advance payment guarantee is a Guarantee example — all real credit-granting instruments, but from the other two methods.

questionBank.q: A bank lends out the cash portion of a customer's deposit to a borrower, who then deposits the loan proceeds into a second bank. Considering both banks' balance sheets together, why does total banking-system assets rise above the original deposit amount?
opts: Because the central bank issues new physical currency each time a loan is disbursed.
Because the borrowed funds become a fresh deposit at the second bank, itself available to lend again.
Because both banks are permitted to report the same funds simultaneously as separate deposits for accounting purposes.
Because the second bank's liquidity reserve requirement is waived for redeposited loan proceeds.
questionBank.exp: The loan proceeds become a genuine new deposit at the second bank, which the worked example above shows growing total bank assets from N100,000 to N175,000 without any new physical currency entering the system — the material is explicit that this new paper is fictitious and not backed by currency at all. Waived reserves and simultaneous double-reporting are both invented exceptions the material does not support.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a Guarantee, one of the three ways banks grant credit?
opts: Term Loan
Performance bond
Trade Finance Facility
Commercial paper
questionBank.exp: A performance bond is listed as an example of a Guarantee. Term Loan and Trade Finance Facility are Direct Lending examples instead, and commercial paper is an Underwriting example — all real instruments, but each belonging to a different one of the three credit-granting methods.

questionBank.q: The borrower who received Zenith Trust Bank's N150,000 cash deposits the full amount into Harbor Bank. If Harbor Bank applies the same 10% Cash Reserve Ratio and 15% liquidity reserve to this new deposit, how much cash does Harbor Bank have available after setting aside both reserves?
questionBank.exp: CRR = 10% x N150,000 = N15,000; liquidity reserve = 15% x N150,000 = N22,500; cash = N150,000 − N15,000 − N22,500 = N112,500. N135,000 and N127,500 each omit one of the two reserves, and N75,000 mistakenly deducts the combined 25% reserve twice.

questionBank.q: Which statement best describes spontaneous finance as a source of bank funds?
opts: It is raised through the issuance of bonds and debentures to institutional investors.
It arises from the bank's day-to-day activities and is usually an insignificant funding source.
It is supplied by shareholders and typically forms only a minor portion of total funds.
It consists of demand, savings, and time deposits collected from the general public.
questionBank.exp: Spontaneous finance is current liabilities arising from the bank's day-to-day activities, and is described as usually an insignificant source of funds. The other three options describe borrowings, equity capital, and deposits respectively — all real, larger funding sources, but distinct from spontaneous finance.

questionBank.q: Harbor Bank lends N90,000 of its available cash to a separate borrower, who then deposits the full loan proceeds into Zenith Trust Bank, where the original N200,000 depositor's funds are still held. What is Zenith Trust Bank's new total deposit liability after this redeposit?
questionBank.exp: Zenith Trust Bank's liability simply adds the new N90,000 deposit to the existing N200,000, giving N290,000. N350,000 mistakenly adds Harbor Bank's full N150,000 deposit rather than the N90,000 actually re-lent and redeposited; N200,000 ignores the redeposit entirely; and N267,500 mistakenly substitutes a later reserve-adjusted cash figure for the actual deposit amount.

questionBank.q: A junior analyst argues that because no new physical cash entered the banking system in this sequence of deposits and loans, total banking-system assets could not really have grown from N200,000 to N350,000 — the growth must be an accounting illusion. Which response best addresses the analyst's claim?
opts: The analyst is correct: total system assets remain N200,000 throughout, and any larger figure reflects a bookkeeping error.
The growth is real: each redeposited loan becomes new, spendable funds for its recipient bank — exactly what fractional-reserve money creation means.
The growth is real, but only because the central bank injected new currency to match each loan disbursed.
The growth is illusory because Harbor Bank's deposit and Zenith Trust Bank's deposit are legally the same funds counted once.
questionBank.exp: The worked example above shows total bank assets rising from N100,000 to N175,000 through exactly this mechanism, explicitly describing the new paper created as fictitious and not backed by currency — the growth is real precisely because it doesn't require new physical cash. Claiming the totals stay flat, or that new currency issuance or double-counting explain the growth, all contradict the mechanism actually described above.

questionBank.q: Which type of bank is described as the lender of last resort and regulates the activities of all other banks?
opts: The Development Bank
The Central Bank
The Merchant Bank
The Investment Bank
questionBank.exp: The Central Bank is described as the Reserve Bank or banker's bank, also referred to as the lender of last resort, and it regulates the activities of all other banks. Development, Merchant, and Investment Banks are all real bank types, but none carries a regulatory or lender-of-last-resort role.

questionBank.q: Which statement correctly describes Non-Interest Banks?
opts: They collect deposits and lend exclusively to members of a single neighbourhood.
They lend to customers without requiring the payment of interest on the facilities extended.
They deal mostly in international finance and do not provide regular banking services to the public.
They are geared towards providing intermediation services to the lower end of the retail market.
questionBank.exp: Non-Interest Banks lend to customers without requiring the payment of interest on their facilities. Lending to a single neighbourhood describes Community Banks, dealing mostly in international finance describes Merchant Banks, and serving the lower end of the retail market describes Microfinance Banks — each a real bank type, but not the one described here.

questionBank.q: A large manufacturing conglomerate regularly draws down multi-billion-naira credit facilities from its bank and rarely holds a net deposit balance. How would this customer be classified using all three customer-segmentation bases together?
opts: A retail, corporate, deposit customer
A wholesale, corporate, borrowing customer
A wholesale, commercial, deposit customer
A retail, consumer, borrowing customer
questionBank.exp: The conglomerate's multi-billion-naira facilities make it a wholesale, corporate-strategy customer, and rarely holding a net deposit balance makes it a borrowing customer by cash-flow generation — together, wholesale, corporate, borrowing. The other combinations each swap in a mismatched label: retail or commercial understates its scale, and deposit customer contradicts a business that rarely holds a net balance.

questionBank.q: Beyond their contribution to a bank's operating revenue, what additional characteristic makes loans especially attractive relative to other assets a bank could hold?
opts: Loans typically carry the lowest risk of default among all bank assets.
Loans are typically the highest-yielding assets a bank can add to its portfolio.
Loans are the only assets that qualify as liquid, near-cash holdings.
Loans are exempt from the cash reserve and liquidity ratio requirements applied to deposits.
questionBank.exp: Loans are described as among the highest-yielding assets a bank can add to its portfolio, with a gross yield no other asset product consistently matches. Loans in fact carry the highest, not lowest, default risk; liquid, near-cash assets describe minimum risk assets like Treasury Bills, not loans; and no exemption from reserve requirements is described anywhere in the material.

questionBank.q: By 2014, total outstanding bank loans in Nigeria exceeded N20 trillion — more than four times the national government's budget for that year. What does this figure most directly illustrate about lending?
opts: Lending had, by that point, become a smaller contributor to bank income than fee-based services.
Lending operates at a scale large enough to function as a driver of overall national economic development.
Lending volumes had permanently exceeded what banks' deposit bases could support.
Lending at that scale indicates government spending had become the primary source of bank deposits.
questionBank.exp: The N20-trillion, four-times-the-budget figure is cited specifically to illustrate lending's role as a driver of overall national economic development, one of the five reasons banks lend. It does not support a claim that fee income overtook lending, that deposit bases were permanently outstripped, or that government spending drove bank deposits — none of those claims appear in the material.

questionBank.q: After several banks merge during a round of industry consolidation, the resulting institution's equity capital comes to represent a noticeably larger share of its total funds than before. Which statement best explains this shift?
opts: Consolidation eliminated the bank's reliance on deposits as a source of funds.
Consolidation raised the ratio of equity capital to a bank's total funds.
Consolidation converted the bank's borrowings into additional demand deposits.
Consolidation is described as having no effect on the composition of a bank's funds.
questionBank.exp: It is noted that the ratio of equity capital to a bank's total funds rose recently due to increased equity from consolidation, even though equity capital still supplies only a minor portion of total funds for most banks. Consolidation is not described as eliminating deposit reliance, converting borrowings into deposits, or leaving fund composition unchanged — the opposite of that last claim is what actually happened.

questionBank.q: Three of the following four services fall within the Central Bank of Nigeria's definition of banking business, and one does not. Which one falls outside that definition?
opts: Receiving deposits on current, savings, or other accounts
Provision of insurance underwriting services
Paying or collecting cheques drawn or paid in by customers
Making or managing investment on behalf of any person
questionBank.exp: Insurance underwriting services fall outside the CBN's definition of banking business — it is separately stated that banks cannot provide insurance underwriting, loss adjusting, or re-insurance services. Receiving deposits, paying or collecting cheques, and managing investment on a person's behalf are all explicitly named within the CBN's definition.

questionBank.q: A mid-sized manufacturer needs project-specific term financing plus assistance underwriting a bond issue in the same relationship, and cannot meet a minimum deposit requirement above a few million naira with its bank. Weighing everything covered on Nigeria's bank types and lending methods, which single arrangement most realistically satisfies all three needs at once?
opts: A Commercial Bank alone satisfies all three needs, since it can lend, underwrite, and has no minimum deposit requirement.
No single bank type satisfies all three needs: only Merchant Banks combine lending with underwriting, but their deposit minimum is too high.
A Community Bank alone satisfies all three needs, since it lends to businesses and has no minimum deposit requirement.
A Merchant Bank alone satisfies all three needs, since its minimum deposit requirement is low enough for this manufacturer.
questionBank.exp: Only Merchant Banks combine lending with the ability to underwrite securities, but they require a minimum deposit of N100 million — far above what this manufacturer can meet — so no single bank type cleanly satisfies all three stated needs at once. Commercial Banks can lend but cannot underwrite; Community Banks serve a defined neighbourhood or cell rather than manufacturers seeking bond underwriting; and Merchant Banks' minimum deposit is a genuine barrier here, not a low one.

questionBank.q: Under BOFIA 2020, what is identified as part of the primary business of a bank?
opts: Underwriting equity shares for corporate clients
Receiving deposits and collecting cheques for customers
Issuing bonds on behalf of the government
Providing insurance underwriting services to customers
questionBank.exp: BOFIA 2020 identifies receiving deposits on current, savings, or similar accounts, and paying or collecting cheques drawn by or paid in by customers, as part of a bank's primary business. Underwriting equity is a Merchant Bank activity, and insurance underwriting is explicitly barred to banks — neither is the BOFIA definition itself, and issuing government bonds is not a bank's own business at all.

questionBank.q: What characterized Nigeria's Free Banking Era, before regulation was introduced in 1952?
opts: Banks operated under strict CBN oversight with mandatory minimum capital requirements.
Banks operated without regulation or capital, causing frequent failures.
The government owned and operated every bank in the country.
International banks were barred from operating in Nigeria entirely.
questionBank.exp: The Free Banking Era was marked by banks operating without regulation and often without strong capital, resulting in frequent bank failures and depositor losses. Strict CBN oversight came later, government ownership of every bank never happened, and international banks were not barred from operating.

questionBank.q: A newly independent nation in the 1950s wants to issue its own national currency, supervise its banking sector directly, and maintain monetary stability, rather than continuing to rely on colonial-era currency arrangements. Which kind of institution addresses all three needs at once?
opts: A merchant bank offering wholesale lending and underwriting services
A central bank, like the CBN, established in 1958
A deposit insurance corporation protecting customer deposits
A private commercial bank focused on retail deposit-taking
questionBank.exp: The CBN was established in 1958 specifically to issue currency, supervise banks, and maintain monetary stability — exactly the three needs described. A merchant bank, a deposit insurer, and a commercial bank are all real institutions, but none issues national currency or sets monetary policy.

questionBank.q: What primarily drove Nigeria's 2004 banking consolidation exercise?
opts: A government decision to nationalize all privately owned banks.
A requirement that banks raise capital, prompting mergers into stronger banks.
The introduction of mobile banking technology across the industry.
The establishment of the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation.
questionBank.exp: The 2004 consolidation exercise required banks to significantly raise their capital base, driving mergers and producing fewer, stronger banks. Nationalization never occurred, mobile banking technology is a later and unrelated development, and the NDIC's establishment predates and is not the cause of the 2004 exercise.

questionBank.q: What is the SANNEF initiative designed to achieve in the Nigerian financial sector?
opts: Regulating the activities of fintech companies operating in Nigeria.
Promoting financial inclusion by expanding agent networks offering basic services.
Reducing the number of licensed deposit money banks in the country.
Setting the Monetary Policy Rate on behalf of the Central Bank.
questionBank.exp: SANNEF (Shared Agent Network Expansion Facilities) promotes financial inclusion by aggressively rolling out agent networks offering basic financial services. It does not regulate fintech companies, reduce the number of licensed banks, or set the Monetary Policy Rate — all separate functions belonging to other bodies or tools.

questionBank.q: A telecom-backed institution offers customers cash-in, cash-out, and funds transfer services through mobile agents, but does not grant loans or accept fixed deposits the way a commercial bank does. What type of institution is this?
opts: A Merchant Bank
A Payment Service Bank
A Non-Interest Bank
A Primary Mortgage Institution
questionBank.exp: A Payment Service Bank offers basic financial services such as cash-in, cash-out, and funds transfer, primarily through mobile channels, without full commercial lending activity — exactly this description. Merchant Banks deal in wholesale finance and underwriting, Non-Interest Banks are defined by lending without interest, and Primary Mortgage Institutions focus on mortgage lending, none of which matches this scenario.

questionBank.q: A company builds a budgeting app that connects to a customer's existing bank accounts to give spending insights, without itself holding any customer funds or offering cash-in/cash-out services. How does this company differ from a Payment Service Bank?
opts: There is no difference; fintech companies and PSBs are simply two names for the same licence category.
It is a fintech company giving technology-based insight, not a licensed deposit-taking or cash-handling PSB.
It is itself a Payment Service Bank, since it deals with financial data.
It is a Merchant Bank, since it targets sophisticated financial customers.
questionBank.exp: Fintech companies use technology to let people digitally access, manage, or gain insight into their finances, without themselves holding funds or handling cash — distinct from a PSB, which is a licensed institution offering cash-in, cash-out, and transfer services. Treating the two as identical, or calling this app a PSB or Merchant Bank, misapplies a licensed-institution label to a pure technology provider.

questionBank.q: A promoter wants to launch a venture that (i) offers basic cash-in/cash-out and transfer services via agents without taking on credit risk, and (ii) eventually underwrites corporate bond issues for established companies. Weighing everything on Nigeria's licensed institution types, can a single licence type cover both ambitions at once?
opts: Yes, a single Payment Service Bank licence covers both ambitions, since PSBs may also underwrite corporate securities.
No: a PSB licence covers the first ambition but can't underwrite bonds; only a Merchant Bank licence permits underwriting.
Yes, a single Merchant Bank licence covers both ambitions, since Merchant Banks also offer basic agent cash-in/cash-out services.
No bank licence in Nigeria permits underwriting corporate bond issues under any circumstances.
questionBank.exp: A Payment Service Bank licence fits the first ambition — basic agent-based cash services without credit risk — but PSBs do not underwrite securities; only a Merchant Bank licence permits underwriting equity and debt issues. Since neither single licence covers both ambitions, the promoter would need two separate licences, not one that does everything, and underwriting itself is very much a real, permitted activity for Merchant Banks.

questionBank.q: A bank fails to meet its new minimum capital requirement under the CBN's 2024 recapitalization circular before the compliance deadline. By which date must banks have completed this requirement?
opts: December 31, 2024
March 31, 2026
March 31, 2025
December 31, 2026
questionBank.exp: Banks must meet the new minimum capital requirements by March 31, 2026, under the 24-month compliance window set by the CBN's 2024 recapitalization circular. The other dates are plausible but incorrect deadlines.

questionBank.q: What is the minimum capital requirement for a National Merchant Bank under the CBN's 2024 recapitalization guidelines?
opts: N15 billion
N50 billion
N20 billion
N100 billion
questionBank.exp: National Merchant Banks must hold a minimum capital of N50 billion. N15 billion was the pre-2024 Merchant Bank figure, N20 billion applies to National Non-Interest Banks, and N100 billion is not a tier used under the current guidelines.

questionBank.q: What is the minimum capital requirement for a Regional Non-Interest Bank under the 2024 recapitalization guidelines?
opts: N5 billion
N10 billion
N20 billion
N50 billion
questionBank.exp: Regional Non-Interest Banks must hold a minimum capital of N10 billion. N5 billion is not the figure for this tier, N20 billion applies to National Non-Interest Banks, and N50 billion applies to Regional Commercial or National Merchant Banks instead.

questionBank.q: What is the minimum capital requirement for a National Non-Interest Bank under the 2024 recapitalization guidelines?
opts: N10 billion
N20 billion
N50 billion
N5 billion
questionBank.exp: National Non-Interest Banks must hold a minimum capital of N20 billion. N10 billion applies to Regional Non-Interest Banks, N50 billion applies to Regional Commercial or National Merchant Banks, and N5 billion is not the figure for this tier.

questionBank.q: A promoter is licensing a new Non-Interest Bank that will operate only within a single geopolitical zone, not nationwide. Under the 2024 recapitalization guidelines, what minimum capital applies?
opts: N20 billion, the National Non-Interest Bank requirement
N10 billion, the Regional Non-Interest Bank requirement
N50 billion, the National Merchant Bank requirement
N5 billion, a figure not used under the current guidelines
questionBank.exp: A Non-Interest Bank operating within a single zone is Regional, requiring N10 billion in minimum capital. N20 billion is the National tier for the same licence type, N50 billion belongs to an entirely different licence category, and N5 billion is not a current Non-Interest Bank figure.

questionBank.q: Three of the following four capital figures are correctly matched to their licence tier under the 2024 recapitalization guidelines, and one is mismatched. Which one is mismatched?
opts: Regional Commercial Bank — N50 billion
National Merchant Bank — N20 billion
International Commercial Bank — N500 billion
Regional Non-Interest Bank — N10 billion
questionBank.exp: National Merchant Bank is mismatched with N20 billion — its actual requirement is N50 billion; N20 billion instead belongs to the National Non-Interest Bank tier. Regional Commercial (N50bn), International Commercial (N500bn), and Regional Non-Interest (N10bn) are all correctly matched.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best summarizes a current issue shaping Nigeria's banking sector today?
opts: A sustained reduction in the number of fintech companies entering the market.
Expanding financial inclusion through agent networks and licensed non-bank channels like PSBs.
A move away from digital channels back toward branch-only banking.
The elimination of Payment Service Banks as a licence category.
questionBank.exp: Expanding financial inclusion through agent networks and channels like Payment Service Banks is a defining current issue in the sector. Fintech entry is growing rather than shrinking, digital channels are expanding rather than retreating, and PSBs remain an active licence category rather than being eliminated.

questionBank.q: A regulator reviews a young bank's progress: it meets its new 2024 recapitalization capital tier on schedule, and separately partners with an agent network under a SANNEF-style initiative to reach underserved customers. How should the regulator read these two developments together?
opts: Negatively, since meeting a capital requirement and pursuing financial inclusion are mutually exclusive goals.
Positively on both fronts: the bank is meeting its capital-strength obligations while also advancing financial inclusion.
Neutrally, since neither development has any bearing on the bank's regulatory standing.
Negatively, since SANNEF-style partnerships are restricted to banks that have failed their capital requirements.
questionBank.exp: Meeting a capital tier on schedule and advancing financial inclusion through agent networks are both genuinely positive, unrelated developments — nothing makes them mutually exclusive, irrelevant to standing, or restricted to under-capitalized banks, none of which the material supports.

questionBank.q: What does the acronym BOFIA stand for?
opts: Bank Operations and Financial Inclusion Act
Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act
Banking Oversight and Fiscal Integrity Authority
Bureau of Financial Institutions and Agencies
questionBank.exp: BOFIA stands for the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act, the key piece of legislation guiding bank activities in Nigeria. The other options are invented names that do not correspond to any real statute or body.

questionBank.q: A customer wants to (i) send a cash transfer through a mobile agent without opening a full bank account, and (ii) use a budgeting app that reads her existing bank transaction data for spending insights, without the app holding any of her money. Which two institution types serve these needs respectively?
opts: A Merchant Bank for (i) and a Non-Interest Bank for (ii)
A Payment Service Bank for (i) and a fintech company for (ii)
A fintech company for (i) and a Payment Service Bank for (ii)
A Primary Mortgage Institution for (i) and a Merchant Bank for (ii)
questionBank.exp: A Payment Service Bank handles agent-based cash transfers without a full account, and a fintech company provides the data-driven budgeting insight without holding funds — matching each need correctly. Merchant Banks, Non-Interest Banks, and Primary Mortgage Institutions serve entirely different purposes, and reversing PSB and fintech swaps which institution does which job.

questionBank.q: Which categories of licensed institutions were assigned new minimum capital tiers under the CBN's 2024 recapitalization circular?
opts: Only Commercial Banks, with Merchant and Non-Interest Banks left unchanged
Commercial Banks, Merchant Banks, and Non-Interest Banks
Only fintech companies and Payment Service Banks
Only Primary Mortgage Institutions and Microfinance Banks
questionBank.exp: The 2024 recapitalization circular set new minimum capital tiers for Commercial Banks, Merchant Banks, and Non-Interest Banks. It did not leave Merchant or Non-Interest Banks unchanged, and it is not aimed at fintech companies, Payment Service Banks, or the Primary Mortgage Institution and Microfinance Bank tiers.

questionBank.q: Minimum capital requirements rose substantially across every Commercial, Merchant, and Non-Interest Bank tier under the 2024 recapitalization. What underlying purpose does this increase serve, consistent with why capital requirements exist at all?
opts: Guaranteeing that every bank will earn a higher annual profit regardless of performance.
Giving banks a bigger buffer to absorb losses and survive financial shocks.
Reducing the number of banking licence categories available in Nigeria.
Eliminating the need for banks to maintain a Cash Reserve Ratio.
questionBank.exp: Capital requirements exist to give banks a buffer to absorb losses and withstand financial shocks, and the 2024 increase simply recalibrates that buffer to a higher standard across the existing tiers. It guarantees no particular profit outcome, leaves the licence categories themselves unchanged, and has no bearing on the separate Cash Reserve Ratio requirement.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best defines financial intermediation as performed by banks?
opts: The process of transferring depositors' funds directly into government treasury accounts.
The process of transferring funds from the surplus sector to the deficit sector.
The process of converting foreign currency into local currency for exporters.
The process of underwriting a customer's securities issue on the capital market.
questionBank.exp: Financial intermediation is the process of transferring funds from the surplus sector (depositors) to the deficit sector (borrowers), using depositors' monies to create loans. Converting currency for exporters and underwriting securities are both real banking functions, but neither defines intermediation itself, and funds are never described as flowing directly into government treasury accounts.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is classified as a Contractual intermediary?
opts: Commercial Banks
Pension Funds Administrators
Investment Management Firms
Finance Houses
questionBank.exp: Pension Funds Administrators (along with life insurance companies) are classified as Contractual intermediaries. Commercial Banks are Depository intermediaries, while Investment Management Firms and Finance Houses are both classified as Investment intermediaries — all real categories, but distinct from Contractual.

questionBank.q: A bank collects many small deposits from individual savers and combines them to fund a single large corporate loan. Which function of financial intermediation does this illustrate?
opts: Transforming money by duration
Transforming money by scale
Transforming money by spatial location
Acting as a risk assessor
questionBank.exp: Collecting numerous small deposits and lending larger amounts to borrowers is exactly how a bank transforms money by scale. Duration transformation concerns short deposits funding long loans, spatial-location transformation concerns connecting distant lenders and borrowers, and risk assessment concerns evaluating and spreading investment risk — none of which this scenario describes.

questionBank.q: A bank accepts mostly short-term savings deposits but extends 20-year mortgage loans to homebuyers. Which function of financial intermediation does this illustrate?
opts: Transforming money by scale
Transforming money by duration
Transforming money by spatial location
Acting as a risk assessor
questionBank.exp: Deposits are mostly short-term while loans are mostly long-term, and financial intermediation overcomes this mismatch by transforming money by duration — exactly what funding a 20-year mortgage from short-term deposits does. Scale transformation concerns combining small deposits into larger loans, spatial-location transformation concerns geographic search costs, and risk assessment concerns evaluating investment risk.

questionBank.q: A saver in Lagos has surplus funds, and a borrower two states away needs financing, but neither would ever locate the other on their own. A bank connects them without either party searching directly. Which function of financial intermediation does this illustrate?
opts: Transforming money by scale
Transforming money by spatial location
Transforming money by duration
Acting as a risk assessor
questionBank.exp: Lenders and borrowers may be unable to find each other even within the same geographical area, and financial intermediation eliminates this cost of searching — transforming money by spatial location. Scale transformation concerns combining small deposits, duration transformation concerns the deposit-loan term mismatch, and risk assessment concerns evaluating investment risk, none of which is the point of this scenario.

questionBank.q: An individual investor with surplus funds lacks the expertise to evaluate the creditworthiness of dozens of potential borrowers, while a bank, operating at much larger scale, can evaluate and spread these risks efficiently. Which function of financial intermediation does this best illustrate?
opts: Transforming money by scale
Acting as a risk assessor
Transforming money by duration
Transforming money by spatial location
questionBank.exp: Banks are better equipped to value the risks of various investments than individual investors, and through their larger scale are also better able to spread those risks — this is the risk-assessor function of intermediation. Combining small deposits describes scale transformation, matching short deposits to long loans describes duration transformation, and neither concerns the credit-evaluation capability this scenario highlights.

questionBank.q: In a Letter of Credit transaction, which party issues the written undertaking to pay the seller?
opts: The Beneficiary
The Issuing Bank
The Applicant
A collecting bank acting purely as an agent
questionBank.exp: The Issuing Bank gives the written undertaking, at the request and on the instructions of the buyer, to pay the seller against stipulated documents. The Beneficiary is the seller receiving the undertaking, the Applicant is the buyer requesting it, and a collecting bank acting purely as an agent describes the very different Bills for Collection arrangement.

questionBank.q: An exporter wants a bank's binding undertaking to pay a stated sum against stipulated documents, rather than relying on the bank merely to hold documents until payment or acceptance of a draft. Which trade-service instrument fits the exporter's requirement?
opts: Bills for Collection
A Letter of Credit
A performance bond
An advance payment guarantee
questionBank.exp: A Letter of Credit is a written undertaking by the issuing bank to pay at sight or a determinable future date against stipulated documents — exactly the binding payment commitment the exporter wants. Bills for Collection instead has the bank act purely as a collecting agent with no payment guarantee; performance bonds and advance payment guarantees are real instruments, but both are Guarantee-category products rather than trade-collection instruments.

questionBank.q: A customer requests a bank-issued cheque, drawn on the bank itself, to make a large one-off payment with guaranteed funds. Which transaction service does this represent?
opts: An Electronic Purse
A Manager's Cheque
An Overseas Transfer
A Standing Order
questionBank.exp: A Manager's Cheque is the transaction service listed for exactly this purpose — a cheque drawn on the bank itself for guaranteed payment. Electronic purses and overseas transfers are real transaction services but serve different purposes, and a standing order is a funds-transfer product for recurring payments, not a one-off guaranteed cheque.

questionBank.q: A construction company must submit a bid guarantee to a government agency as a precondition for tendering on a public contract. Which of the bank's guarantee products fits this requirement?
opts: An Advance Payment Guarantee
A Bid Bond
A Bankers' Acceptance
A Commercial Paper Guarantee
questionBank.exp: A Bid Bond is the guarantee product listed for exactly this purpose — supporting a tender bid. Advance payment guarantees instead cover funds paid in advance of performance, bankers' acceptances are a separate underwriting-adjacent instrument, and commercial paper guarantees relate to backing a commercial paper issue, not a public tender.

questionBank.q: A Nigerian importer needs foreign currency to pay an overseas supplier. How does the importer's bank typically source this foreign currency?
opts: By issuing a bid bond on the importer's behalf.
By making a bid to the central monetary authority.
By borrowing the foreign currency from a correspondent bank's treasury reserves.
By converting the importer's naira deposits directly at the interbank placement rate.
questionBank.exp: The importer's bank sources the needed currency by making a bid to the central monetary authority. A bid bond is an unrelated guarantee product for tenders, and borrowing from a correspondent bank's reserves or converting deposits at an interbank placement rate are both invented mechanisms this specific process does not describe.

questionBank.q: A Nigerian exporter receives payment in US dollars for goods shipped abroad. What does the exporter's bank do with these dollar proceeds?
opts: It converts the dollars into Treasury Bills on the exporter's behalf.
It credits the naira equivalent of the foreign currency into the exporter's account.
It forwards the dollars unconverted directly into the exporter's domiciliary account only.
It requires the exporter to sell the dollars back to the original importer directly.
questionBank.exp: The exporter receives the foreign currency through the bank, which credits the local currency equivalent into the client's account. Converting to Treasury Bills, forwarding dollars unconverted, or requiring a direct resale to the importer are not how this process is described.

questionBank.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a floating exchange rate from a fixed exchange rate?
opts: A floating rate is determined by government fiat, while a fixed rate is determined by market forces.
A floating rate is determined by market forces, while a fixed rate is determined by government fiat.
Both rate types are determined by the same central monetary authority bid process.
A floating rate applies only to spot transactions, while a fixed rate applies only to forward transactions.
questionBank.exp: A floating exchange rate is determined by the interplay of market forces, while a fixed rate is determined by government fiat — the first distractor simply reverses this. The central monetary authority bid process concerns how banks source currency, not how the rate itself is set, and rate regime is independent of whether a given transaction is spot or forward.

questionBank.q: China administers its currency's value primarily through government fiat rather than market interplay. Most other countries instead allow market forces to determine their currency's value. What does this contrast best illustrate?
opts: The difference between a spot market transaction and a forward market transaction.
The difference between a fixed and a floating exchange rate regime.
The difference between direct lending and underwriting as credit-granting methods.
The difference between a Depository intermediary and a Contractual intermediary.
questionBank.exp: Government fiat versus market-force determination of a currency's value is precisely the distinction between a fixed and a floating exchange rate regime, with China cited as the fixed-rate example. Spot versus forward markets concern settlement timing, not rate-setting, and the other two options misapply unrelated classifications from other topics entirely.

questionBank.q: A trader agrees today to exchange currencies at today's quoted rate, with the funds due to change hands within two business days. Which foreign exchange market does this transaction belong to?
opts: The forward market
The spot market
The interbank placement market
The commercial paper market
questionBank.exp: The spot market quotes exchange rates for transactions delivered at immediate value, usually within two business days — exactly this transaction. The forward market instead deals with delivery at a specific future date, and interbank placements and commercial paper are real money-market instruments unrelated to FX settlement timing.

questionBank.q: A Nigerian company knows today that it must pay a foreign supplier in US dollars six months from now, and wants to lock in today's exchange rate to eliminate the risk of naira depreciation before then. Which foreign exchange arrangement should the company use?
opts: A spot market transaction, since it settles within the usual two-business-day window.
A forward market contract, since it fixes delivery of value at a specific future date.
A floating exchange rate policy, since it allows the rate to adjust with market forces.
A fixed exchange rate policy, since government fiat guarantees rate stability going forward.
questionBank.exp: The forward market deals with delivery of value at a specific future date, letting the company lock in today's rate for a payment due in six months. A spot transaction settles almost immediately, not six months out; a floating-rate policy is the opposite of locking in a rate; and a fixed exchange rate is a national policy stance set by government fiat, not an arrangement an individual company can adopt for one transaction.

questionBank.q: A bank manages a client's money through a portfolio of shares, bonds, and cash equivalents, according to the client's stated investment objectives. Which bank function does this describe?
opts: Custodial services
Asset management
Portfolio articulation
Financial advisory services
questionBank.exp: Asset management is the process of managing money for individuals through shares, bonds, or cash equivalents, according to stated objectives or investment styles — exactly this activity. Custodial services instead concern safekeeping physical instruments, portfolio articulation concerns advising on a portfolio's construction rather than managing it directly, and financial advisory services cover a different set of activities such as M&A and restructuring.

questionBank.q: A bank advises a client on how to build and manage an investment portfolio within a set of specific constraints the client has defined, without directly managing the client's money itself. Which investment-management activity does this describe?
opts: Asset management
Portfolio articulation
Custodial services
Underwriting
questionBank.exp: Portfolio articulation within specified constraints focuses on advising customers on how to build and manage their portfolio of investments — an advisory role, distinct from asset management, which involves directly managing the client's money. Custodial services concern safekeeping rather than advice, and underwriting is an unrelated credit-granting method.

questionBank.q: A company stores its physical share certificates and title documents with its bank for safekeeping, paying a fee for this service. Which bank function does this represent?
opts: Asset management
Custodial services
Financial advisory services
Trade services
questionBank.exp: Custodial services provide vault services for the safekeeping of physical instruments and valuables, including safekeeping and settlement of title documents to financial securities, for a fee — exactly this scenario. Asset management and financial advisory services involve managing money or giving strategic advice rather than safekeeping documents, and trade services concern import/export payment facilitation instead.

questionBank.q: A business considering a debt-for-equity restructuring seeks the bank's guidance on how best to structure the transaction. Which bank function provides this kind of guidance?
opts: Custodial services
Financial advisory services
Monetary policy function
Trade services
questionBank.exp: Financial advisory services include advising businesses exploring restructuring opportunities, such as capital restructuring or debt conversion, executed through the bank's Corporate Finance department. Custodial services and trade services are unrelated safekeeping and import/export functions, and the monetary policy function concerns implementing national monetary policy, not advising individual businesses.

questionBank.q: A state government wants to sell its majority stake in a public utility to private investors and asks its bank to structure and manage the sale. Which category of financial advisory service does this fall under?
opts: Mergers and acquisitions advisory
Privatization or divestiture advisory
Debt restructuring advisory
Standalone valuation advisory
questionBank.exp: Financial advisory services explicitly include advisory services for privatization, divestiture, or joint venture partnership — exactly what selling a government stake to private investors describes. Mergers and acquisitions advisory concerns combining companies rather than a government selling a stake, and debt restructuring and standalone valuation advisory are real but separate categories listed alongside this one.

questionBank.q: Which set of tools does a bank use, in partnership with monetary authorities, to help implement the country's monetary policy?
opts: Capital Adequacy Ratio, Single Obligor Limit, and Deposit Insurance
Cash Reserve Ratio, Liquidity Ratio, and Open Market Operations
Letters of Credit, Bills for Collection, and Bankers' Acceptances
Asset Management, Custodial Services, and Financial Advisory Services
questionBank.exp: The monetary policy function is carried out through the Cash Reserve Ratio, the Liquidity Ratio, and Open Market Operations, in partnership with monetary authorities and government. Capital Adequacy Ratio, the Single Obligor Limit, and Deposit Insurance are real regulatory tools covered elsewhere but serve prudential supervision rather than monetary policy, while the other two sets are trade instruments and investment services respectively, unrelated to monetary policy.

questionBank.q: A bank channels government-directed credit to specific priority sectors of the economy on behalf of a government agency, rather than deciding independently which sectors to lend to. Which role is the bank performing?
opts: Acting as an issuing bank under a Letter of Credit
Acting as an on-lending intermediary for credit allocation
Acting as an underwriter of a government bond issue
Acting as a custodian of government securities
questionBank.exp: Banks work with government to achieve credit allocation by acting as on-lending intermediaries, channeling directed credit to targeted sectors rather than choosing independently. Issuing a Letter of Credit, underwriting a bond issue, and acting as a securities custodian are all real bank roles, but none describes channeling government-directed credit on an agency's behalf.

questionBank.q: A conglomerate asks its bank, in a single relationship, to (i) safeguard its bearer share certificates, (ii) advise on acquiring a competitor, and (iii) manage its short-term treasury bill holdings according to stated return objectives. Which three bank functions, in order, does this require?
opts: Custodial services, portfolio articulation, and trade services
Custodial services, financial advisory services, and asset management
Financial advisory services, asset management, and monetary policy function
Trade services, underwriting, and financial advisory services
questionBank.exp: Safeguarding certificates is custodial services, advising on an acquisition is financial advisory services (mergers and acquisitions), and managing treasury bill holdings against stated objectives is asset management — covering all three requests in order. The other combinations each substitute in a function, such as portfolio articulation, trade services, underwriting, or the monetary policy function, that doesn't match one of the three specific requests described.

questionBank.q: Which three areas make up the Depository category of financial intermediaries?
opts: Finance Houses, Investment Management Firms, and Merchant Banks
Corporate Banking, Commercial Banking, and Retail/Consumer Banking
Pension Funds Administrators and Life Insurance Companies
Islamic Financial Institutions and Non-Interest Banks
questionBank.exp: Depository intermediaries comprise Corporate Banking, Commercial Banking, and Retail/Consumer Banking. Finance Houses and Investment Management Firms are Investment intermediaries instead, Pension Funds Administrators and Life Insurance Companies are Contractual intermediaries, and Islamic Financial Institutions and Non-Interest Banks are real bank types from a different classification entirely.

questionBank.q: How does financial intermediation benefit both lenders and borrowers at the same time?
opts: It guarantees lenders a fixed return regardless of a borrower's repayment performance.
It ensures liquidity for both sides: lenders can call in funds, and borrowers have ready funding.
It requires borrowers to repay only once the original lender personally requests repayment.
It removes the need for banks to evaluate a borrower's creditworthiness before lending.
questionBank.exp: Financial intermediation always ensures liquidity for both lenders and borrowers — lenders can call in their funds, and borrowers have a ready source of funding for their needs. No fixed-return guarantee is described, repayment isn't tied to the original lender's personal request since the bank itself intermediates, and banks are in fact described as better equipped to assess borrower risk, not exempt from doing so.

questionBank.q: A Letter of Credit specifies that payment is due to the beneficiary at a determinable future date rather than immediately upon presentation of documents. What does this indicate about the issuing bank's undertaking?
opts: The issuing bank is no longer obligated to pay once documents are presented.
The issuing bank agreed to pay on that later date, not immediately at sight.
The transaction has effectively become a Bills for Collection arrangement instead.
The beneficiary must now seek payment directly from the applicant instead of the bank.
questionBank.exp: A Letter of Credit is a written undertaking to pay at sight or at a determinable future date — choosing the future-date option simply means the bank's binding commitment falls due later, not that the commitment disappears. The bank remains obligated regardless of timing, the arrangement doesn't convert into a Bills for Collection, and the beneficiary still looks to the issuing bank, not the applicant, for payment.

questionBank.q: Three of the following four are among the four functions financial intermediation performs, and one is not. Which one is not?
opts: Transforming money by scale
Guaranteeing borrowers will never default
Transforming money by duration
Acting as a risk assessor
questionBank.exp: Guaranteeing borrowers will never default is not one of the four functions of financial intermediation — no such guarantee is described anywhere in the material, and risk assessment explicitly acknowledges that default risk exists and must be evaluated, not eliminated. Transforming money by scale, by duration, and acting as a risk assessor are three of the four genuine functions.

questionBank.q: An exporter uses a Bills for Collection arrangement, under which the bank holds shipping documents until the buyer pays or accepts a draft. If the buyer simply refuses to pay, what risk does the exporter bear?
opts: The bank must compensate the exporter directly, since it holds the shipping documents.
The exporter bears the loss, since the bank neither guarantees nor enforces payment here.
The issuing bank is obligated to honor payment, as it would under a Letter of Credit.
The buyer's own bank must reimburse the exporter automatically.
questionBank.exp: Under Bills for Collection, the bank acts purely as a collecting agent, holding documents until payment or acceptance — it does not guarantee payment or enforce collection, so the exporter bears the loss if the buyer refuses to pay. This is precisely the risk a Letter of Credit is designed to remove, since there the issuing bank itself is obligated to pay; no automatic reimbursement from the buyer's bank is described.

questionBank.q: A contractor requires an upfront mobilization payment from a client before starting a construction project, and the client wants assurance the funds will be used properly or refunded. Which guarantee product addresses the client's concern?
opts: A Bid Bond
An Advance Payment Guarantee
A Bankers' Acceptance
A Commercial Paper Guarantee
questionBank.exp: An Advance Payment Guarantee is the product listed specifically for this purpose — protecting a client who has paid funds in advance of performance. A Bid Bond instead supports a tender bid, and Bankers' Acceptances and Commercial Paper Guarantees relate to entirely different instruments, not upfront mobilization payments.

questionBank.q: Letters of Credit appear both among trade services and among guarantee products. What best explains why the same instrument is grouped under both categories?
opts: It is a data-entry duplication, since a Letter of Credit is purely a trade-service instrument with no guarantee element.
A Letter of Credit both facilitates a trade transaction between buyer and seller and functions as the issuing bank's guarantee of payment.
It is a data-entry duplication, since a Letter of Credit is purely a guarantee product with no trade-facilitation role.
